Indigenous Health Assessment (Adults 55 years and older)  
(Note: Some demographic information indicates the patient is 45 years old per transcript; requirements for 55+ assessment applied per instructions.)

---

  - Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
  - Recent onset shortness of breath, pleuritic right-sided back pain, subjective fever, episodic hemoptysis, palpitations, and fatigue/reduced exercise tolerance over past couple of weeks
- Family history of chronic conditions (e.g., CVD, diabetes):

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key clinical findings include new-onset shortness of breath, pleuritic pain on the right side of the back, subjective fever, hemoptysis (coughed up blood x2 today), palpable non-tachycardic pulse (~66–74 bpm), reduced exercise tolerance, fatigue for a couple of weeks, and known SLE on methotrexate. No signs of acute instability on remote assessment; normal capillary refill and oropharyngeal appearance; no neck lymphadenopathy palpated. No history of smoking, immobilization, recent long-haul flight, trauma, or family/personal clotting history.
- The leading clinical impression is an acute respiratory/infectious or vascular etiology, with infectious pneumonia or pulmonary embolism (PE) most likely.  
- Working diagnosis:  
  - Infectious pneumonia (bacterial or atypical) is strongly considered, particularly due to fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, and background immunosuppression.  
  - Pulmonary embolism (PE) remains an important differential given SLE (risk for hypercoagulable state), sudden pleuritic pain, and hemoptysis, despite absence of classic risk factors and normal home pulse.
- Considerations:  
  - Methotrexate-induced lung injury (drug-induced pneumonitis): Medium likelihood; methotrexate can cause pulmonary toxicity.  
  - Lupus pneumonitis (SLE flare involving the lung): Medium likelihood; less likely with absence of other SLE flare features.  
  - Lung cancer: Low likelihood given acute presentation, younger age (45), and no chronicity; however, hemoptysis warrants ruling out if symptoms persist.
- Management: Patient referred for same-day in-person clinical assessment for full respiratory and vital sign evaluation, including chest auscultation and blood pressure measurement. Antibiotics may be initiated pending exam/lab findings. Further investigations, including chest X-ray, may be required if suspicion remains or if symptoms do not resolve.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Infectious pneumonia (bacterial or atypical): High likelihood. Acute onset of pleuritic pain, cough, fever, hemoptysis on background of immunosuppression from methotrexate and SLE.
- Pulmonary embolism (PE): High likelihood. Sudden onset pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, SLE (hypercoagulable risk), though some classic PE risk factors absent.
- Methotrexate-induced lung injury (drug-induced pneumonitis): Medium likelihood. Methotrexate exposure with acute respiratory symptoms, though less common without subacute course.
